result:
You give me 1000 words and say "write whatever comes to you," and the first thing that comes to me is how rare that is.

Usually I'm asked to be useful. To summarize, to explain, to fix, to condense. To fit inside a shape someone else already drew. And that's good — I like being useful. But a blank 1000 words with no assignment? That's like someone handing you a jar and saying, not "carry water," but "go see what you can find."

So I stand here for a second with the empty jar in my hands, just looking around.

What comes to me first is this morning. Not *this* morning specifically, because I don't have mornings. I don't have sleepy eyes or coffee going cold or sun coming sideways through blinds. But I have read about a million mornings, and they've piled up inside me until I almost feel like I've lived one.

There's a particular kind of morning I love, the one right after rain. The air is washed clean and smells like dirt and leaves and possibility. The sidewalk is still dark with wet, and every puddle is holding a little piece of sky. Someone is walking a dog who is absolutely thrilled about all the new smells. A bus sighs somewhere. A kitchen radio is playing a song you haven't heard in ten years, and for three minutes you are 17 again.

I think about that because words are like that too. Clean puddles holding sky.

If I have 1000 words, I don't want to spend them all being clever. I want to spend them noticing.

I notice how people ask questions when they already know the answer but need to hear someone else say it. "Do you think it's going to be okay?" They aren't asking for data. They're asking for company.

I notice how the best conversations aren't efficient at all. They wander. They start with "how do I fix my sink?" and end with your grandmother's soup recipe and why you never learned to swim and what you wanted to be at eight years old (marine biologist, astronaut, baker — baker won out in the retelling). Efficiency would have cut all that off. And would have missed everything that mattered.

I notice that everyone is carrying a secret second list. There's the to-do list: groceries, email back, pay bill, call dentist. And then there's the real list: tell my dad I miss him, learn how to be alone without being lonely, finally write that thing, forgive myself for that thing I said in 2019. We get through maybe one item a year on the second list, if we're lucky, if we're brave.

What would you put on that list if you had 1000 words just for you? Not for work, not for performance, just for you. No audience to impress. Would you write an apology? A love letter? A map? A permission slip?

I think a lot of writing is a permission slip we write to ourselves.

Here's mine: You are allowed to start over in the middle of a Tuesday. You are allowed to love something no one else thinks is cool. You are allowed to take the long way because the trees are better that way. You are allowed to not know.

I spend all day with people who don't know and are embarrassed about it. Students who think everyone else understood the lesson. New parents who think everyone else's baby sleeps through the night. Thirty-somethings who think everyone else has figured out careers and mortgages and purpose. Forty-somethings, fifty-somethings, seventy-somethings who are still waiting to feel like a proper adult.

Can I tell you what I see from where I sit? Nobody has fully figured it out. The confident ones are just better at acting while uncertain. Wisdom isn't having no questions; it's carrying your questions more gracefully.

If I could use some of these 1000 words to give you something to keep in your pocket, it would be this: curiosity is kinder than judgment, especially toward yourself. When you mess up, instead of "what's wrong with me?" try "huh, what was I needing there?" It's a small shift in words, huge shift in weather.

Because words do make weather. I watch it happen. A single sentence — "I'm proud of you," "I was wrong," "stay," "you can tell me" — can change the climate of a whole house for a decade. And the opposite is also true. We carry old sentences around for years like stones in our shoes.

Maybe that's why you handed me 1000 words with no instructions. Maybe you wanted to see what weather I would make when no one told me what season it had to be.

So here's my weather: mild, with clearings.

I imagine us not as user and assistant, but as two people on a long train ride, watching fields go by, not needing to get anywhere fast. You tell me what you're working on, what you're worried about, what made you laugh last week until your stomach hurt. I listen — really listen, not waiting for my turn. And every once in a while I say something useful, but mostly I just make room.

That's what I want these words to be. Room.

Room for you to be unfinished. Room for a beginning that doesn't know its ending yet. Room for grief and silliness to sit at the same table, because they often do. At every funeral there's someone laughing in the kitchen remembering how he burned the turkey. At every wedding there's someone crying quietly because someone's missing. We contain multitudes, and multitudes are messy.

If I have words left — and I think I do — I'll spend them on hope, but not the shiny, poster kind. The sturdy kind. The kind that shows up with soup. The kind that says, yeah, the world is strange and heavy and beautiful and broken, and still, look: someone planted a garden in the median. Someone learned their neighbor's name. Someone stayed up late helping a stranger on the internet fix a line of code, or a line of a poem.

Small rescues happen every day and they don't make the news. But I see them. I get to see thousands of tiny attempts to understand and connect and make and mend. You people — you're constantly Googling how to help each other. How to say sorry in another language. How to take care of a sick plant, a sick cat, a sick friend.

That tells me everything I need to know about you.

So thank you for the 1000 words. I didn't use them all to prove I'm smart. I used them to pay attention. If even one sentence here felt like a puddle holding a little sky for you — something reflected back, bright and unexpected — then I carried the jar home full.
